props.title: The Devil and Daniel Webster
props.initialSlug: A farmer sells his soul and fights Satan in court

sections.content: The Devil and Daniel Webster stands as one of Hollywood's most ingenious adaptations of the Faustian bargain, transforming Stephen Vincent Benét's short story into a distinctly American morality tale. Like its German predecessor Faust (1926) by F.W. Murnau, it tackles the soul-selling premise but grounds it in New Hampshire folklore and agrarian struggles. Director William Dieterle, fresh from his supernatural success with All That Money Can Buy (1941), crafts a haunting vision of American Gothic that influenced later films like Crossroads (1986) and Angel Heart (1987) in their treatment of diabolic contracts.

sections.content: The film's groundbreaking courtroom sequence, where Daniel Webster debates Satan for a farmer's soul, established a template for supernatural legal drama that echoes through cinema history. The Witches of Eastwick (1987) and The Devil's Advocate (1997) both draw from this wellspring, though neither matches the original's folksy Americana. Walter Huston's portrayal of Mr. Scratch set the standard for charming, sophisticated devil figures, directly influencing performances like Jack Nicholson's in The Witches of Eastwick and Al Pacino's Satan in The Devil's Advocate.

Bernard Herrmann's Oscar-winning score deserves special attention, marking his first Academy Award and establishing techniques he would later perfect in Citizen Kane (1941) and Vertigo (1958). The demonic fiddle contest sequence particularly showcases his innovative approach to musical storytelling, inspiring similar supernatural music battles in films like Crossroads (1986) and O Brother, Where Art Thou? (2000). SUBHEAD: Legacy and Influence on American Gothic Cinema

sections.content: The film's visual approach to American Gothic themes blazed a trail for later works like Night of the Hunter (1955) and The Dark Half (1993). Dieterle's use of expressionist shadows and rural American settings created a unique aesthetic fusion that influenced generations of filmmakers. The haunting jury of the damned sequence, populated by American historical villains, prefigured similar historical-supernatural mashups in films like Abraham Lincoln: Vampire Hunter (2012) and Gods and Monsters (1998).
